title: The Language of Sustainable Diets: A Field Study Exploring the Impact of Renaming Vegetarian Dishes on U.K. Café Menus
authors: Linda Bacon; Jonathan Wise; Sophie Attwood; Daniel Vennard
summary: A field experiment in a chain of cafés in the United Kingdom tested which menu language leads more eaters to choose plant-based dishes. Compared with names that highlighted the absence of meat, such as "meat-free" or "vegetarian," names that emphasized taste or origin (such as "Cumberland-spiced") or used appealing words for plant-based options (such as "field-grown" or "garden") significantly increased sales of the target vegetarian dishes. General positive words like "better" or "feel good" had no significant effect. The authors encourage foodservice managers to test more appealing names, an easy and inexpensive way to make menus more sustainable.

title: Association Between Indulgent Descriptions and Vegetable Consumption: Twisted Carrots and Dynamite Beets
authors: Bradley P. Turnwald; Danielle Z. Boles; Alia J. Crum
summary: A research letter on a study in a large Stanford University cafeteria that served about 600 diners each weekday lunch. Over 46 days, one featured vegetable each day was labeled in one of four ways (basic, healthy restrictive, healthy positive, or indulgent) with no change to how it was prepared or served. Indulgent labels led 25% more diners to choose the vegetable than basic labels and 41% more than healthy restrictive labels. The authors conclude that the flavorful, exciting descriptions usually reserved for less healthy foods can increase vegetable consumption.

title: Consumers underestimate the emissions associated with food but are aided by labels
authors: Adrian R. Camilleri; Richard P. Larrick; Shajuti Hossain; Dalia Patino-Echeverri
summary: Two studies on how well eaters understand the climate impact of food. In the first, participants significantly underestimated the energy use and greenhouse gas emissions of foods, which the authors call a blind spot suited to intervention. In the second, labels that expressed a food's life-cycle emissions in a familiar unit, minutes of running a light bulb, shifted actual purchases away from higher-emission options. The authors conclude that a well-designed carbon label is a promising, simple intervention.

title: Food labeling and eco-friendly consumption: Experimental evidence from a Belgian supermarket
authors: Pieter Vlaeminck; Ting Jiang; Liesbet Vranken
summary: A framed field experiment in a Belgian supermarket on whether eaters buy more eco-friendly food when information about a product's environmental impact is easier to use. An online survey first picked the most accessible of six label designs, some of which added a single overall environmental score. In the experimental market, that label made purchases about 5.3% more eco-friendly than the label the supermarket already used, and it also beat a label that showed the raw environmental data.

title: Increasing Vegetable Intake by Emphasizing Tasty and Enjoyable Attributes: A Randomized Controlled Multisite Intervention for Taste-Focused Labeling
authors: Bradley P. Turnwald; Jaclyn D. Bertoldo; Margaret A. Perry; Alia J. Crum; and others
related: Menus of Change University Research Collaborative; Stanford University
summary: A preregistered intervention at five university dining halls in the United States tested whether taste-focused labels increase vegetable intake compared with health-focused labels. Across 137,842 diner decisions, 185 days, and 24 types of vegetables, taste-focused labels increased vegetable selection by 29% compared with health-focused labels and by 14% compared with basic labels, and vegetable consumption also rose. Expectations of a positive taste experience explained the effect, which was larger where the vegetable recipes were tastier. Taste-focused labels outperformed labels with merely positive words, fancy words, or lists of ingredients.
